endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is important to clarify whether the implementer team’s organization monitors and sunsets AI algorithms that are no longer supported and assess whether there is a plan for handling developer-driven EOL processes.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Prior to sunset, organizations should assess the operational, clinical, and workflow impacts of removal and ensure appropriate transition planning, communication, and data handling.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for minimizing disruptions and harms that result from decommissioning AI products and disseminating information about AI product updates to affected clinicians.

evidence.title: Radiology staff perspectives after decommissioning an artificial intelligence (AI) tool for expedited lung cancer triage
evidence.outcome: Staff reliance on and disappointment about withdrawn AI triage tool after decommissioning
evidence.effect: Among reporting staff, 40% (2/5) were disappointed to no longer use the tool and 20% (1/5) reported reliance; 70.0% still believed AI improved patient care; 35% recalled logistical issues.
evidence.quote: Among reporting staff, 40% (2/5) were disappointed to no longer use the tool, while 20% (1/5) reported reliance on it.

evidence.title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence Off-Boarding in Radiology: Staff Perspectives on Decommissioning and a Proposed Withdrawal Framework
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Staff reliance, perceived clinical loss and operational relief after AI tool withdrawal
evidence.effect: Of 40 respondents, 35% perceived logistical burden post-decommissioning; among 5 reporting staff, two voiced disappointment at withdrawal and one had grown reliant on the tool; free text showed both loss of clinical value and operational relief.
evidence.quote: Response rate from reporting staff was low (5 of 40), with two voicing disappointment in AI tool withdrawal, and one stating they had grown reliant on the tool.

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether AI retirement plans reduce care disruption when a tool is withdrawn, although four frameworks recommend such planning. Two reports, which appear to describe the same UK survey of 40 radiology staff, found that some staff had relied on a withdrawn triage tool and that 35% recalled logistical burden afterward.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The two hazard reports share a setting, a sample of 40, and their findings, and they likely represent one survey reported twice. The reliance figures rest on 5 reporting staff, which makes them imprecise. The descriptive design cannot link withdrawal to patient outcomes.

One of 5 reporting staff had grown reliant on the tool, and 35% of 40 respondents recalled logistical issues after withdrawal. This suggests that removing a tool can disturb workflow. Neither report measured missed findings, delays, or patient harm during the transition. The severity of harm is therefore unknown, and no study shows that backup arrangements catch errors.

Free-text responses described both a loss of clinical value and operational relief after decommissioning. This suggests that reliance varies across users, so a retirement plan may need to assess it by role. No study reports the workload of assessing reliance, activating backups, or communicating with staff, so how these steps perform in real workflows is untested.

The four endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks from NIST and CHAI plus a decision-point guide. They use "should" or descriptive language and create no legal duties. The CHAI guide asks whether organizations have a plan for end-of-life processes driven by the developer. That question places part of retirement planning in vendor contracts.

Thirty-five percent of 40 respondents recalled logistical burden after withdrawal, while some free text described operational relief. This mix suggests that decommissioning carries staffing and workflow costs that planning may anticipate. No study reports the cost or staff time needed to maintain retirement plans, so this evidence cannot show whether the practice is feasible at scale.

Both reports surveyed staff only. Seventy percent of respondents still believed the AI had improved patient care. No study asked patients whether they noticed the withdrawal, knew whom to contact, or experienced delays. The evidence does not show whether retirement communication reaches patients or preserves their access to a human.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI withdrawals that followed a structured retirement plan with withdrawals that did not. Such a study could measure turnaround times, missed or delayed findings, staff workload during the transition, and whether patients received information about alternatives and contacts.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The two hazard reports surveyed UK radiology staff and did not describe any Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The evidence therefore cannot show whether harms from withdrawal, or the benefits of retirement plans, differ for these populations, whose backup capacity and communication needs may differ.
